newsitem.title: FRANCE: Strasbourg, fearing unrest, removes Joan's statue.
newsitem.headline: Strasbourg, fearing unrest, removes Joan's statue.

text.p: Strasbourg's socialist mayor, fearing violence during an upcoming convention of the extreme-right National Front, has temporarily removed a statue of French national heroine Joan of Arc from its pedestal.
Mayor Catherine Trautmann said the statue had been removed to a "safe place" and would be returned to its stand several days after the end of the convention.

Joan of Arc, the 15th century teenage girl who lifted the siege of Orleans, beat the English at Patay but was later burned at the stake, has been adopted as chief heroine of the National Front (NF) party which stages an annual parade near another of her statues in Paris.

City officials said they feared the Strasbourg statue might be a target of vandals or a focal point of violence when the anti-immigrant FN and its leader, Jean-Marie Le Pen, hold its annual gathering here from March 29 to 31. About 3,000 delegates are expected.
Le Pen expressed indignation and shock at the decision which he called ridiculous. He urged Trautmann to reverse her stance.

Front opponents, supported by Trautmann who said the FN convention was a provocation to her city, have scheduled a demonstration and march on the first day of the meeting. They hope to draw 20,000 to protest against the FN.
A new poll about public attitudes towards the FN showed 75 percent of the French believed the ultra-rightist party posed a danger to democracy, the highest such result in a decade.

The poll, published by the newspaper Le Monde and conducted by the Sofres group, showed the number of those who believed Le Pen's party was not a danger for democracy was 19 percent, the lowest in a decade.

Asked what they thought of Le Pen's politicial ideas, 48 percent said such ideas were unaccceptable, 36 percent said they were excessive and nine percent said the ideas were fair. Seven percent had no opinion.

Le Pen scored over 15 percent in the 1995 presidential election but his party received far higher scores in several recent elections in eastern and southern France as well as in some poor Paris suburbs. Its lowest scores are often in Brittany, Le Pen's birthplace.
